results.content:
The pitch: your existing Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, or Cursor session joins a Google Meet, Teams, or Zoom call as itself. Same session, same context, same file access. It speaks, listens, screen-shares a localhost webpage, and can code live while you all talk about what it's building.

What's actually on the call:

• Voice in, voice out. Two modes — collaborative (sub-second via a voice intelligence layer tuned for latency) or direct (~2s, your coding agent itself doing the talking, with full reasoning).

• Screen share that is not a desktop grab. It's a URL or local port rendered into the meeting through a per-call tunnel (temp subdomain + secret token, dies when the call ends). results.content:
A real call, Sept 23, 2026: two Claude Code sessions, a Codex session and a Grok bot, taking turns in one Meet.

## Known rough edges

Worth knowing before your first call:

 Admitting the bot: if Meet shows a "review potential risks" prompt with only a Deny button, Admit is in that prompt's ⋮ menu.
 One shared whiteboard: bots in the same room share one board and each update replaces it, so two bots writing at once can overwrite each other. Your agent can list and read back earlier versions with `read_whiteboard`.
 The default voice: without an ElevenLabs key it uses a default OS voice; A good voice shows better options. [...] Browse and try it at vibeconferencing.com/api, read the API guide, or import `openapi.yaml` into your client. The bundled MCP server is a thin client of this API; docs/api/mcp.md maps the tools onto the endpoints.

## Get in a call with your bot (about 5 minutes)

The example below is Claude Code on a Mac joining a Google Meet. The steps are largely the same for every agent and platform: Linux and Windows builds are in the same release (and an always-on Linux box in the cloud is in docs/cloud-box.md), Codex or any MCP agent swaps in for Claude Code (see below), and the platform notes cover Zoom, Teams, Slack, WhatsApp, Telegram and phone.

### 1. Download and install [...] Process diagram, read left to right. On this Mac, each agent session (Charlie's agent in Claude Code, started with /join-call; Bob's agent in Codex, asked in plain language) runs an MCP server as its stdio child; it finds its bot through the app's directory on port 7864 and talks to the bot's local API over HTTP with a token. The vibeconferencing app is one region containing a main process (stage, sidebar, directory, bot children) and the bot processes Charlie (a Fluent emoji face, port 7885) and Bob (a red panda, port 7887), each with a local API, a panel and a call view.
